subject: European History
title: 2. The Concert of Europe and Congress of Vienna

segments.text: After Napoleon, the great powers built a diplomatic order designed to prevent both a renewed French hegemony and revolutionary upheaval — understanding why it worked when powers agreed and weakened when nationalism divided them is the topic’s central analytical task.

The Congress of Vienna (1814–15) sought a stable balance of power, security against renewed French expansion, and restoration of legitimate dynasties where practical, compensating victorious powers with territory. France returned to broadly pre-revolutionary frontiers, the Netherlands was strengthened, Prussia gained Rhineland territory, Austria regained influence in Italy, and Russia expanded in Poland — a map deliberately designed to prevent any single state from dominating Europe again, not simply a restoration of the pre-1789 map.

Congress meetings at Aix-la-Chapelle, Troppau, Laibach and Verona addressed occupation, revolution and intervention, with Britain increasingly resisting the continental powers’ broad claims to a right of intervention against revolutions elsewhere.

The post-1815 order prevented another general European war for decades and brought France back into great-power diplomacy, with consultation helping manage several crises without immediate continent-wide conflict. Its weaknesses became apparent as nationalism, liberal revolutions, and conflicting interests in Spain, Italy, Greece and the Ottoman world exposed real disagreement among the powers — the Concert was a method of diplomacy, not a permanent government of Europe, and it worked far better when great powers agreed on threats than when national and liberal movements divided them.

items.text: The general diplomatic practice of great-power consultation following 1815, distinct from any single formal alliance.
Two distinct 1815 instruments — a practical great-power security pact, and a more ideological monarchical declaration — often confused with each other.
Draw the 1815 territorial settlement; prepare goals, instruments, successes and weaknesses as distinct sections.
Practise one analytical outline answering: “Why did the Concert of Europe succeed in preventing general war for decades, yet fail to contain nationalism and liberalism permanently?”
Do not treat “Concert of Europe,” “Holy Alliance” and “Quadruple Alliance” as identical institutions.
Do not say the Vienna settlement simply restored the old map; important territorial changes were deliberately made.
Do not claim the Concert failed immediately; it contributed to decades of relative great-power stability despite later divisions.
The Congress of Vienna met in 1814–15 after the Napoleonic wars.
Austria’s Metternich became a leading defender of conservative monarchical order.
The Quadruple Alliance linked Britain, Austria, Prussia and Russia; France later re-entered great-power diplomacy.
The Concert reduced the risk of another general European war for decades but could not suppress nationalism and liberalism permanently.
The core formula for this topic is balance of power plus great-power consultation plus conservative reaction, followed by growing disagreement over intervention and nationalism.
Vienna’s territorial settlement was a deliberate anti-hegemonic design, not a simple restoration — a nuance worth stating explicitly.
